questions.stem: An average-risk adult asks the nurse for a single cancer-screening schedule that would apply unchanged for the rest of life. Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Screening depends on age, anatomy, prior results, and individual risk factors, so recommendations should be matched to the person and updated over time.","B":"Once one screening test is negative, further screening for that cancer is unnecessary unless the client later develops symptoms suggesting disease.","C":"All asymptomatic adults should receive the same cancer tests at the same intervals because screening recommendations are intentionally risk-neutral for every age.","D":"Cancer screening should begin only after symptoms appear because testing asymptomatic people creates more harm than benefit across all cancer types."}}
questions.rationale: Evidence-based screening recommendations vary by cancer type and depend on age and individual risk. A fixed lifelong schedule for every adult is inaccurate; screening should follow current recommendations and be individualized when risk factors or prior findings change.
questions.source_name: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — Recommendation Topics
questions.source_detail: USPSTF recommendations are organized by preventive service and population, with age and risk criteria specific to each screening recommendation.

questions.stem: Parents of a healthy 2-month-old ask how to reduce sleep-related infant death risk. Which sleep setup should the nurse recommend?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the infant prone on a firm mattress without pillows because prone positioning improves comfort when loose bedding is removed.","B":"Use a slightly inclined sleep surface with a positioning pillow because elevation reduces regurgitation without increasing sleep-related risk.","C":"Place the infant supine on a separate firm, flat, noninclined sleep surface with a fitted sheet and no soft objects or loose bedding.","D":"Bed-share with a nonsmoking caregiver on an adult mattress because close observation offsets the hazards associated with shared sleep surfaces."}}
questions.rationale: AAP guidance recommends supine positioning for every sleep, a firm flat noninclined sleep surface, and removal of soft objects and loose bedding. Room-sharing on a separate infant sleep surface is safer than routine bed-sharing.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Safe Infant Sleep Recommendations
questions.source_detail: AAP recommends back-to-sleep, a firm flat noninclined surface, and no soft objects or loose bedding.

questions.stem: A client who recently lost a job and relationship says, “I don't see the point of any of this anymore,” then looks away. What should the nurse do next?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Change the topic briefly and wait for the client to raise the subject again so direct questioning does not unintentionally increase suicide risk.","B":"Offer reassurance that the losses are temporary before asking about safety because positive reframing is the best first step in a formal suicide assessment.","C":"Ask only whether the client feels depressed, because asking directly about suicide can introduce an idea that was not previously present.","D":"Ask directly and calmly whether the client is thinking about suicide or self-harm, then continue a structured safety assessment based on the answer."}}
questions.rationale: Directly asking about suicidal thoughts does not cause or increase suicidal thinking and is an appropriate way to identify a person at risk. A concerning statement should be explored rather than minimized, deferred, or replaced by reassurance.
questions.source_name: NIMH — Frequently Asked Questions About Suicide
questions.source_detail: NIMH states that asking directly about suicide does not increase suicidal thoughts and can be the best way to identify someone at risk.

questions.stem: A client with a trauma history becomes visibly anxious when told a nonemergent procedure must happen immediately without explanation. Which response best reflects trauma-informed care?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Explain what will happen, promote physical and emotional safety, and offer meaningful choices about timing or process when clinically feasible.","B":"Avoid discussing the client's concerns and proceed quickly because minimizing conversation reduces the chance of retraumatization during procedures.","C":"Use the same communication style for every client because adapting care to prior trauma creates inconsistent treatment and weakens boundaries.","D":"Remove as much control as possible from the client so the procedure can be completed efficiently before anticipatory anxiety increases further."}}
questions.rationale: SAMHSA's trauma-informed approach emphasizes safety, trustworthiness, collaboration, and empowerment, voice, and choice while seeking to resist retraumatization. Clear explanation and meaningful choice are appropriate when the situation is not emergent.
questions.source_detail: SAMHSA identifies safety, trustworthiness/transparency, collaboration/mutuality, and empowerment/voice/choice as core principles.

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder praises one nurse as “the only person who understands me,” then calls the same nurse “awful” after a limit is set. Which pattern is the nurse observing?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sublimation, in which an unacceptable impulse is redirected into an activity that is safer or more socially acceptable to the individual.","B":"Splitting, in which the same person is viewed in sharply polarized all-good or all-bad terms rather than as having mixed qualities.","C":"Reaction formation, in which a person behaves in a way that is opposite to an unacceptable underlying feeling or impulse.","D":"Rationalization, in which a person constructs a plausible explanation to make an uncomfortable action or feeling seem more acceptable."}}
questions.rationale: The rapid shift from idealizing to devaluing the same person is consistent with splitting, a pattern of polarized perception commonly associated with borderline personality disorder. It differs from rationalization, sublimation, and reaction formation.
questions.source_detail: Clinical references describe splitting and marked shifts between idealization and devaluation as characteristic patterns in borderline personality disorder.
